label: Arepas
definition: Flat-metal cooking: dry heat with total contact, no walls, no steam trap. The COMAL (Mexican, carbon steel or clay): tortillas puffed (the recipe wing's flour-tortilla law), chiles and tomatoes charred for salsas (the blister IS the flavor: dry-charring is a technique category), quesadillas sealed. The PLANCHA (Spanish) and TEPPAN (Japanese): restaurant flat-tops delivering full-surface Maillard. Smash burgers' entire physics (maximum crust contact), gambas a la plancha, fried rice at scale. Home translation: a carbon-steel griddle or the cast-iron pan's flat side across two burners; outdoor flat-top grills (the Blackstone era) brought plancha cooking to backyards. The flat-top's professional edge: heat ZONES across one surface, sear left, hold right, the pass's geography in steel.

label: Asado fire
definition: Three fires, three clocks. GRILLING: direct high heat, minutes, for tender cuts: the two-zone setup (hot side/cool side) is the entire skill, giving sear and refuge in one grate. BARBECUE: indirect low heat (105–135°C) plus wood smoke, hours, for collagen cuts (brisket, shoulder, ribs) where 'low and slow' is the collagen conversion clock wearing an apron. SMOKING divides again: hot-smoking cooks while flavoring; cold-smoking (under ~30°C) flavors cured foods without cooking. Thin blue smoke good, white billows bitter; the fire is an ingredient and must be cooked as carefully as the meat.

label: Béchamel: the mother sauce
definition: The thickener's toolkit. ROUX: equal weights flour and fat cooked together: white (2 min) for béchamel, blond for velouté, brown to brick-dark for gumbo, each stage trading thickening power for flavor. SLURRY: cornstarch or arrowroot in cold water, whisked into simmering liquid at the end: instant gloss, Asian-sauce standard, breaks down if boiled long. LIAISON: egg yolk and cream tempered in off the heat: the silk finish of blanquette and avgolemono; boil it and you've made sweet scrambled regret. BEURRE MANIÉ: raw butter-flour paste whisked in at the finish, the braise-rescuer. Choose by the sauce's temperature future, not habit.

label: Beurre blanc
definition: REDUCTION: simmering a liquid to evaporate water, concentrating flavor and body, the sauce-maker's primary move, always reduced BEFORE final seasoning (salt concentrates too). NAPPE: the classical doneness test: sauce coats the back of a spoon and holds a clean line drawn by a finger. MONTER AU BEURRE: 'mounting' cold butter cubes into a finished sauce off the heat, swirling, emulsifying in gloss, body, and richness; the last thirty seconds that make restaurant sauces taste like restaurant sauces. Together they are the grammar of à-la-minute saucing: reduce, season, mount, plate.

label: Blanching & shocking
query: blanch and shock technique ice bath
definition: Brief boiling in heavily salted water followed by an ice-bath arrest. It sets chlorophyll's electric green (and stops it there), softens vegetables to exact tenderness for later reheating (the restaurant à-la-minute secret: nearly everything green was blanched hours ago), loosens skins (tomatoes, peaches, fava), and tames raw edges (onion for salads). The salt matters: it seasons and protects color; the shock matters more: residual heat keeps cooking anything not stopped. Blanch-and-shock is the technique that lets a ten-minute dinner service plate a two-hour mise.

label: Braising
definition: Combination cooking: sear for Maillard flavor, then simmer partially submerged (braise, big pieces) or fully submerged (stew, small pieces) in a covered pot at a bare tremble (85–95°C liquid, oven around 150°C) until collagen converts to gelatin. The conversion needs time above ~70°C, which is why tough cuts get tender and lean cuts get dry: choose collagen-rich muscle always. Universal laws: never boil (boiled braises are grainy), skim honestly, rest overnight when possible (flavor marries, fat lifts), and the strained liquid IS the sauce: reduce and mount it, waste nothing.

label: Brining & curing
definition: Salt's three levels of commitment. WET BRINE (5–8% salt solution, hours): dissolves some muscle protein so meat retains water: juicier lean cuts, diluted flavor, wet skin. DRY BRINE (salting 1–3 days ahead, uncovered): seasons deeply, keeps flavor concentrated, and desiccates skin for crackling, the modern professional default for poultry and steaks. CURING (higher salt, often with nitrite, plus time): preservation and transformation. Bacon, gravlax, pastrami, prosciutto. The through-line is diffusion and osmosis given time; 'season early' is the shortest version of this entire entry.

label: Building an emulsion
definition: Fat and water convinced to coexist as droplets, held by an emulsifier (egg-yolk lecithin, mustard, starch, or sheer agitation): the physics behind mayonnaise, hollandaise, vinaigrette, beurre blanc, aioli, and glossy pan sauces. The universal method: add fat SLOWLY to the water phase while shearing hard; the universal failure: too fast, too hot, or too cold, and it 'breaks' into grease. The universal rescue: start fresh with a new yolk (or a spoon of water/mustard) and whisk the broken sauce INTO it. Pasta's starchy water emulsifying oil and butter into clinging sauce is the same trick; Italian kitchens just never named it.

label: Butchery basics
definition: FRENCHING: scraping rib bones clean (racks of lamb, tomahawks, crown roasts), pure presentation, honest theater. BUTTERFLYING: splitting a piece horizontally almost through and opening it like a book: even thickness for fast cooking (chicken breasts) or a canvas for stuffing (roulades, porchetta). TYING: butcher's twine at intervals to hold shape. Even cooking, clean slices. SILVERSKIN: the iridescent membrane that never renders; strip it from tenderloins with a knife-tip and a pull. These verbs are where cooking begins before heat exists; a chef who butchers understands the animal a recipe can't teach.

label: Charring over open flame
query: charring vegetables chilies over flame technique
definition: The browning reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars, roaring above ~140°C, the source of seared steak crust, bread crust, roasted coffee, fried onions, and toasted anything: hundreds of new flavor compounds from one bit of chemistry. Its enemies are water (surfaces must be DRY: a wet steak steams at 100°C forever) and crowding (which traps steam). Its friends: high heat, dry surfaces, a little alkalinity (the pinch of baking soda in stir-fry velveting and pretzel dips). Distinct from CARAMELIZATION, which is sugar alone breaking down at ~160°C+. Half of 'flavor' in savory cooking is engineering these two reactions on purpose.

label: Churning ice cream
definition: Ice cream is texture engineering, small ice crystals plus controlled air (overrun), and the machines are crystal-size strategies. HOME CHURNERS: frozen-bowl (cheap, one batch, pre-freeze the bowl 24h) vs. self-refrigerating compressors (batch after batch, the enthusiast's line). The pastry-science levers travel with either: sugar and alcohol depress freezing (scoopability), fat carries flavor, stabilizers (or the custard wing's egg base) manage melt; churn cold bases fast, harden in shallow containers. The pro disruptors: the PACOJET spins FROZEN solid blocks into instant micro-shaved creams to order (savory sorbets, herb ices, single-portion economics, a fine-dining fixture), and its consumer descendant (the Ninja Creami class) brought the same shave-don't-churn idea home, remaking the category. Kulfi (the dessert wing) reminds everyone the no-machine road exists: density as a choice. Whatever the hardware: the base recipe is 80% of the result: machines only preserve the texture you formulated.

label: Churros
definition: Frying is violent dehydration: oil at 160–190°C flash-boils surface moisture outward (the bubbles ARE water leaving), creating crust while steam-cooking the interior. Laws: recover temperature between batches (crowding = greasy), match oil to job (neutral high-smoke oils for deep; the double-fry, low then high, for fries, tostones, and chicken that must stay crisp), drain on RACKS not paper (paper steams the base), and salt in the first seconds while the surface is still hot and receptive. Oil is a reusable ingredient: strain it, smell it, retire it when it darkens or foams.

label: Creaming butter & sugar
query: creaming butter sugar cake structure technique
definition: Cakes rise on air you built before the oven. CREAMING: beating butter and sugar until pale: sugar crystals literally cut air pockets into the fat, which chemical leaveners then inflate (butter cakes, cookies where the long cream = lift). FOAMING: whipping eggs (whole: genoise; whites: meringue, angel food, chiffon) into a protein foam, the sponge family's entire structure. RIBBON STAGE: whole eggs and sugar whipped until the batter falls in a slowly-dissolving ribbon, the doneness test for sponges and molten cakes alike. The corollary rule: once air is in, FOLD, never stir: every rough stroke is height surrendered.

label: Dashi
definition: WHITE STOCK: raw bones, gentle simmer: clean, pale, for velouté and light soups. BROWN STOCK: bones and mirepoix roasted first, tomato paste caramelized: deep color and roasted flavor, the mother of demi-glace and jus. BROTH is meat-based and seasoned to drink; stock is bone-based, unsalted, and built for gelatin. A proper stock sets like Jell-O cold. GLACE is stock reduced to a syrup; a spoon flavors a whole pan sauce. Skim relentlessly, never boil (cloudiness is emulsified scum), salt never (it concentrates downstream), and know that stock is the bank account every other station borrows from.

label: Deglazing & pan sauces
definition: FOND (French for 'base/foundation') is the browned glaze of proteins and sugars welded to the pan after searing, concentrated Maillard flavor that amateurs scrub into the sink and professionals convert into money. DEGLAZING: pouring liquid (wine, stock, even water) into the hot emptied pan and scraping; the fond dissolves into an instant sauce base. From there: reduce, season, mount with butter, and a sautéed anything becomes a finished dish. The habit to build: never wash a pan with fond in it until you've asked what sauce it wanted to become.

label: Draining fried food: a rack, never paper
query: draining fried food rack technique crisp
definition: Frying's equipment truth: the vessel is simple; the DISCIPLINE is the machine. Home setups ranked: a heavy DUTCH OVEN with a clip thermometer (thermal mass = temperature stability, the recovery physics of the frying entry) beats most countertop electric fryers (underpowered, slow recovery); a WOK fries with less oil and more surface; dedicated electric fryers earn space only with filtration and frequency. The management protocol that separates operations from accidents: never past two-thirds full, food DRY (water is the eruption), a spider and a landing rack staged BEFORE the first drop, baking soda or a lid for fire (never water: say it twice), and oil husbandry: strain through fine mesh after each session, store dark and cool, track uses by what was fried (fish retires oil fastest), retire at darkening, foaming, or off smells. Air fryers, honestly filed: compact convection ovens: excellent at reheating fried food and roasting small batches, incapable of actual frying; useful appliance, dishonest name. Restaurant note: fryer oil is a tracked COST line and a fire-code fixture: respect it at home like the pros are required to.

label: Dry-pan toasting: spices, seeds and nuts
definition: The smallest technique with the largest per-second flavor return: dry heat waking pyrazines and oils in anything with fat and starch to brown. THE METHODS ranked: OVEN (160–175°C on a sheet pan) for volume and evenness: nuts 8–12 min, stirred once; STOVETOP DRY PAN for small batches and whole spices: constant motion, trust your nose over your eyes (fragrant means nearly done; golden means done; 'one more minute' means starting over); the aggressive exception: coconut and sesame toast in a blink and burn in the next. THE LAWS: toast WHOLE then chop (surface-area math: chopped pieces scorch at the corners), carryover is real (pull a shade early; hot nuts keep cooking on the pan: decant immediately), toasted flavors FADE in liquid (re-toast garnishes; add toasted elements late), and salt while warm when salting at all. THE APPLICATIONS threading this guide: the nutty register's entire pantry, dukkah and gomasio, toasted-rice powder for larb, the pie crust's blind-baked depth, spices before grinding, and the honest truth that most 'flat' granola, pesto, and praline died of raw nuts. When in doubt, toast, but stand there while you do.

label: Egg wash & the baker’s shine
definition: Three ways of painting with heat. BASTING: spooning pan juices or fat over roasting food: flavor and sheen, though evidence says its moisture claims are romance; it mostly speeds surface cooking and pleases the cook. ARROSER: the French pan ritual: tilting the pan and spoon-showering foaming butter, garlic, and thyme over a steak or fish in its final minute: aroma infusion plus a butterfat crust. GLAZING: painting reduced sauces (teriyaki, barbecue, honey-mustard) in THIN repeated coats late in cooking so sugars lacquer instead of burn, the huli huli and yakitori law. Sugar burns at the temperature meat browns; timing is the technique.

label: Fermentation
definition: Two preserved-sour families the menu should distinguish. QUICK PICKLING: vinegar, sugar, salt poured over: sour today, no microbes involved. LACTO-FERMENTATION: salt (2–3% by weight) suppresses bad microbes while lactobacillus converts sugars to lactic acid (sauerkraut, kimchi, real dill pickles, curtido), living sour with depth vinegar can't fake. Adjacent kingdoms: KOJI (Aspergillus mold on rice/barley) powers miso, soy sauce, and modern dry-age shortcuts; yeast ferments bread and beer; SCOBYs make kombucha and vinegar itself. Ferments are how a restaurant builds house flavor no supplier can sell the competition.

label: Filleting fish
query: how to fillet a fish technique
definition: Blades that follow anatomy. BONING (5–6", stiff or semi-flex): rides bones and seams: breaking down chickens, frenching racks, seaming out silverskin; the stiff version muscles through joints, the flexible sweeps curves. FILLET (6–9", fully flexible): the fish specialist bending along the spine, skinning in one drawn stroke. Japan's specialists: HONESUKI: the triangular poultry-boning knife whose pointed authority converts chicken breakdown from chore to craft; DEBA: the thick single-bevel cleaver-knife that heads and fillets whole fish (spine chopped by the heel, flesh drawn by the edge). Butchery blades are where sharpening pays cash: yield percentage (see the menu-economics entry) is literally a function of edge and angle: a sharp boning knife is a raise you give yourself.

label: Flambé
definition: Directed fire, sold as a dessert toy and worth far more. The canon: CRÈME BRÛLÉE's glass lid (thin sugar, even sweeps, let it cool to glass: the pastry wing's stage-managed caramel), meringue toasting (baked Alaska's peaks, tarte au citron's optional crown). The savory second life: peeling peppers and tomatoes in place, blistering shishitos, finishing sous-vide proteins' edges where the pan can't reach (the crevices of a chicken thigh, a roast's pale corner: torch as detail-sear), melting cheese to order, aburi-style sushi's kissed fat (torched salmon nigiri's entire genre), charring citrus for cocktails. Hardware truth: the tiny culinary torches are underpowered toys; a hardware-store propane or MAP-gas head with a trigger igniter costs less and works properly; hold the flame so food sees the blue cone's TIP, keep it moving, and mind the 'torch taste' (unburned fuel from too-close, too-rich flames: distance and a hot, lean flame prevent it).

label: Fresh pasta
definition: Gluten is the elastic network formed when wheat's glutenin and gliadin meet water and agitation: the structure of bread, the enemy of tenderness in cakes and pie crusts. The baker steers it three ways: FLOUR CHOICE (bread flour ~12–14% protein builds; cake flour ~8% barely does), FAT (shortens gluten strands, hence 'shortening', 'shortbread', 'shortcrust'), and TECHNIQUE (kneading develops it; minimal mixing and resting relax it). HYDRATION is water as a percentage of flour weight: 60% is a tight bagel dough, 75% a country loaf, 85%+ the wet ciabatta school. Baker's percentages, everything relative to flour at 100%, are the professional language; learn them and every formula scales.

label: Knife cuts: dice, julienne, bias
query: classical knife cuts brunoise julienne technique
definition: The French system exists because even cuts cook evenly and plate professionally. The ladder: BRUNOISE (3mm dice) and its baby FINE BRUNOISE (1.5mm); JULIENNE (matchsticks 3mm × 5cm) and BATONNET (6mm × 6cm, the fry); small/medium/large DICE (6/12/20mm); PAYSANNE (thin tiles); CHIFFONADE (herbs and leaves rolled and sliced into ribbons); TOURNÉ (the seven-sided football that has hazed culinary students for a century). MINCE is fineness without geometry; SUPREME is the citrus segment freed from all membrane. Speed comes later; uniformity is the exam, and the claw grip is the tuition.

label: Lamination
definition: Folding a butter block into dough and rolling repeatedly to create alternating sheets, dozens to hundreds of layers, so oven heat turns the butter's water to steam and jacks the layers apart: croissants, puff pastry, danish, kouign-amann, and the medialuna's method. The disciplines: dough and butter at matched plasticity (cold but bendable: shattered butter means leaks; warm butter means brioche), rest between folds (gluten relaxes or it fights back), and counted turns (3 letter-folds ≈ 27 layers; 6 ≈ 729 for classic puff). 'Rough puff' cheats with butter chunks and honest speed. Lamination is pastry's showpiece of the principle that structure IS technique.

label: Marinating: acid, salt and time
definition: VELVETING is the Chinese restaurant's tenderness secret: sliced meat coated in egg white, cornstarch, and a little baking soda or wine, rested, then pre-cooked briefly in oil or water; the alkaline soda relaxes surface proteins and the starch jackets in moisture, producing that signature silk in stir-fries. MARINADES, honestly assessed: salt, sugar, and acid work only millimeters deep (oil carries aromatics to the surface); enzyme marinades (pineapple, papaya, yogurt's gentler lactic action) genuinely tenderize but turn meat mushy past their window. Marinades are surface seasoning plus browning chemistry: the flavor is real; the 'penetration' is mostly myth, and the dry brine outperforms for depth.

label: Mashing & puréeing
definition: Three machines, three physics, endless substitution errors. IMMERSION (stick) BLENDER: purées IN the pot: soups without lava transfers (the soup wing's blend-smooth entries assume one), mayo in 60 seconds (the one-jar immersion-mayo trick), sauce rescues; the restaurant version is a boat motor. HIGH-SPEED BLENDER (Vitamix-class): the smoothness ceiling: velvet soups, nut butters, silky salsas and curry bases (heat from friction is real: it will warm and even cook contents; also the reason it emulsifies like a champion). FOOD PROCESSOR: the CHOPPER: pulse-control texture (pesto with identity, pie dough's butter pebbles, falafel's coarse grind, shredding discs at volume) where blenders would liquefy. The sorting rule: liquids and smoothness → blender; solids and texture → processor; in-pot and quick → stick. And the professional footnote: the blender's whirl adds AIR: sauces that must stay glossy-dense (the mortar entry's argument) sometimes want the pound or the pass instead.

label: Pie crust & blind baking
definition: BLIND BAKING: baking a crust empty (lined with parchment and weighted with beans/rice/sugar) before a wet filling arrives: partial for quiches that bake again, full for cream and citrus tarts. DOCKING: pricking pastry so steam escapes flat where puff isn't wanted. The pie-crust catechism: cold fat in visible pieces (steam pockets = flake), minimal water, minimal handling (gluten = toughness), rest before rolling, chill before baking (cold pastry into a hot oven holds its architecture). A 'soggy bottom' is the genre's public shame; the defenses are blind baking, a hot steel or stone below, egg-wash waterproofing, and fillings added no wetter than they must be.

label: Poaching eggs

label: Steaming: basket, leaf and lid
definition: Cooking in vapor at 100°C: gentler than boiling (no agitation, no flavor leached into water) and the technique of choice where the ingredient IS the dish: Cantonese fish, dim sum, couscous, tamales, Christmas pudding. label: Straining & passing through a sieve
definition: Texture's final gatekeepers: the difference between good and restaurant-smooth is usually a pass through mesh. label: Sugar stages & caramel

Wet caramel (sugar + water) is safer; dry caramel is faster and riskier. Crystallization is the saboteur: don't stir once boiling, brush down stray crystals, or insure with corn syrup/glucose. Add cream and butter and it's sauce; add nothing and stop it dark and it's the top of a crème brûlée's ancestry.

label: The broiler: heat from above
definition: Heat from above: the finisher's station. label: The tagine
definition: The oldest cookware still winning on merit: clay heats slowly, radiates gently and evenly, holds warmth to the table, and (unglazed) breathes moisture in a way metal cannot. definition: The thermometer is the truth (that entry stands), but the senses are the always-on instruments, and professionals read both. label: Tortillas on the comal

definition: Flat-metal cooking: dry heat with total contact, no walls, no steam trap. The COMAL (Mexican, carbon steel or clay): tortillas puffed (the recipe wing's flour-tortilla law), chiles and tomatoes charred for salsas (the blister IS the flavor: dry-charring is a technique category), quesadillas sealed. The PLANCHA (Spanish) and TEPPAN (Japanese): restaurant flat-tops delivering full-surface Maillard. Smash burgers' entire physics (maximum crust contact), gambas a la plancha, fried rice at scale. Home translation: a carbon-steel griddle or the cast-iron pan's flat side across two burners; outdoor flat-top grills (the Blackstone era) brought plancha cooking to backyards. The flat-top's professional edge: heat ZONES across one surface, sear left, hold right, the pass's geography in steel.

label: Trussing
definition: FRENCHING: scraping rib bones clean (racks of lamb, tomahawks, crown roasts), pure presentation, honest theater. BUTTERFLYING: splitting a piece horizontally almost through and opening it like a book: even thickness for fast cooking (chicken breasts) or a canvas for stuffing (roulades, porchetta). TYING: butcher's twine at intervals to hold shape. Even cooking, clean slices. SILVERSKIN: the iridescent membrane that never renders; strip it from tenderloins with a knife-tip and a pull. These verbs are where cooking begins before heat exists; a chef who butchers understands the animal a recipe can't teach.

label: Velveting
definition: VELVETING is the Chinese restaurant's tenderness secret: sliced meat coated in egg white, cornstarch, and a little baking soda or wine, rested, then pre-cooked briefly in oil or water; the alkaline soda relaxes surface proteins and the starch jackets in moisture, producing that signature silk in stir-fries. MARINADES, honestly assessed: salt, sugar, and acid work only millimeters deep (oil carries aromatics to the surface); enzyme marinades (pineapple, papaya, yogurt's gentler lactic action) genuinely tenderize but turn meat mushy past their window. Marinades are surface seasoning plus browning chemistry: the flavor is real; the 'penetration' is mostly myth, and the dry brine outperforms for depth.

label: Whipping a meringue

definition: One foam, three temperaments. FRENCH: raw whites whipped with sugar; lightest, least stable, for baking into pavlova shells and folding into batters. SWISS: whites and sugar warmed over a bain-marie to ~70°C then whipped, denser, glossier, safe from grit, the buttercream base. ITALIAN: 118°C sugar syrup streamed into whipping whites: fully cooked, the most stable of all, for torching (baked Alaska, tarte au citron meringuée) and marshmallow work. Universal laws: no trace of yolk fat, a clean bowl, sugar added gradually, and 'stiff peaks' means the tip stands with a slight bow; chalky over-whip is one minute past glory.

label: Wok technique
definition: Wok hei, 'the breath of the wok', is the smoky, singed-air aroma from food and oil vaporizing against carbon steel at extreme heat, micro-charring in mid-toss. The home translation: maximum burner, a carbon-steel wok preheated to smoking, ingredients DRY and cut uniform, everything prepped before ignition (a stir-fry is 90% mise, 10% cooking), small batches, sauces poured down the hot wok wall so they scorch-caramelize on arrival, and the discipline of letting food SIT between tosses to catch char. Crowding is the killer; one portion at a time is the law from char kway teow to pad see ew.
